How much to charge for mold remediation

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$999 mold special.” That number is not a takeoff. An 80-square-foot closet with one containment zone and one equipment day is not the same job as an 800-square-foot finished basement with two zones, four dry-out days, 240 square feet of demo, and a clearance. The word “mold job” is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the containment and the demo, not just the special

Basement-waterproofing calculators price wells, a pit, and discharge. Radon-mitigation calculators price suction, membrane, and circuit. Pest-control calculators price bait stations. Drywall calculators price hang-and-finish of new board. A mold job is a contained remediation: the included closet, the extra zone the special never mentions, the demolition, the equipment days, and the clearance. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first extra zone eats the field margin.

A job with a similar first zone can cost much more

Each extra zone is poly, a zipper, and a negative-air setup that never appears on the brochure. Extra square feet over the included closet are billed as their own hours. Demo, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, occupied-home access, and a third-party clearance are adders that get forgotten on a closet special. On the sample rates an 800 sq ft finished basement with two zones, four dry-out days, 240 sq ft of demo, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, occupied access, and a clearance prices about $11,543 ($14.43 per square foot of affected area, 39.0 crew-hours). The same shop’s 80 sq ft closet prices about $1,724 ($21.55 per square foot, 6.3 hours, walk-away $1,207). Matching a $3-per-square-foot internet quote on the basement is how that job becomes a loss of about $5,680.

A sewage-backed room is not automatically the expensive one

A 400 sq ft category-3 sewage-backed room with two zones, 200 sq ft of demo, three equipment days, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, occupied access, and a clearance is not the basement plus 20%. On the sample rates that sewage job prices about $9,333 ($23.33 per square foot, 32.0 crew-hours) — more per square foot than the basement, less as a total, because the extra 400 basement squares and the extra dry-out day do not live in a published sewage adder. A typical 200 sq ft bedroom with 40 sq ft of demo and two dry-out days prices about $2,948 (10.5 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first extra zone.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $45/h tech loaded at 36% payroll burden is $61.20. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample rates even the brochure closet walk-away is $1,207, which is why a $999 Facebook special is already a loss of about $208 before the first extra zone. Replace every rate with your HEPA invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a mold inspection, a health determination, a clearance certificate, a guarantee that any building will test below a spore or moisture threshold, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Job type, affected area, containment zones, demolition, and whether the house needs a third-party clearance are yours to confirm.

Price your next job

Common questions

How much to charge for mold remediation?

Charge from the included closet, extra square feet over that include, extra containment zones, demolition, HEPA and dehumidifier days, third-party clearance, HVAC cleaning, dumpster, occupied-home access, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 80 sq ft closet at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $1,724 — about $21.55 per square foot of affected area.

Why is a flat mold-special quote dangerous?

Homeowners count 'a mold job is a mold job.' Extra containment, demolition, equipment days, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, and a third-party clearance do not live in a $999 special. Matching a cheaper closet quote written for a brochure bath is how a finished basement becomes a loss.

Does a larger house always cost more to remediate?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates an 800 sq ft finished basement with two zones, four dry-out days, 240 sq ft of demo, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, occupied access, and a clearance prices around $11,543 ($14.43 per square foot), while an 80 sq ft closet prices around $1,724 ($21.55 per square foot).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not mold, environmental, construction, health, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and kit rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a mold protocol, or a health determination — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Common questions

      How can anyone advertise a "$999 mold special"?

      Because it is written for one small job, and that job is a preset here: an 80 sq ft closet, one containment zone, one equipment day, no demo, no clearance, no dumpster, unoccupied. At that scope the number is real. An 800 sq ft finished basement with two zones, four dry-out days, 240 sq ft of demo, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, third-party clearance, and a family living in the house is a different job in eight separate places. Price both side by side and the conversation with the homeowner stops being about who is cheaper.

      Why is affected area charged "past an included amount" instead of per square foot?

      Because a flat $/sq ft misprices both ends. A remediation has a fixed cost of showing up at all — set-up, the first containment, the first equipment day — that a per-foot rate has to smear across the job. Here the base setup and the first containment are their own lines, and only area past the included amount adds hours, per 100 sq ft. Extra containment zones work the same way and carry their own kit cost, because a second zone is a second poly build, not a bigger version of the first.

      Why is dry-out priced on the longer of HEPA days and dehumidifier days?

      Because the crew's calendar is set by whichever piece of equipment is on site longest, not by the sum. Labor hours follow that longer figure. Equipment rental, though, is billed per unit per day, so HEPA days and dehumidifier days are each costed separately at their own daily rate. Adding the two for labor would double-count the same days on site; adding them for rental is correct, because two machines really are two rentals.

      What does an occupied home add?

      Its own hours line. Working around a family means more protection, more moves, more re-explaining, and a shorter productive day inside containment. It is entered as a toggle with its own hours rather than folded into a rate, so you can see what it costs and decide whether to schedule around it. Clearance testing, HVAC cleaning, and a dumpster each work the same way — a toggle with its own hours and its own fee, because all three cost time as well as money.

      Is this a mold protocol or a health assessment?

      No, and it must not be used as one. This is bid arithmetic on numbers you type. It is not a remediation protocol, an inspection, a health or safety determination, a clearance criterion, or an opinion on whether any particular growth is hazardous. Scope, containment design, and clearance standards come from your assessor, your jurisdiction, and the applicable standard of care — this page prices the work someone else has already scoped.

      Why isn't a 25% margin the same as adding 25% to my cost?

      Margin here is a share of the final price — price = total cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the customer and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $5,000 cost marked up 25% is $6,250, a 20% margin; a 25% target margin is $6,667. Everything stays in this browser: no account, no upload, "Forget my business details" clears the proposal details, and the optional local counter records only which features were used and the day.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

vs-a-flat-999-mold-special.html.text:
← Mold Remediation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $999 mold special

“$999 mold removal” is not a price for a remediation job — it is a price for one specific 80 sq ft closet, quietly applied to every mold call that comes in.

What a flat $999 mold special is

A flat price is the fastest number a company can put on a postcard, a search ad, or a lead-gen page: one price, no inspection, easy for a homeowner to compare between bids. It works as a lead magnet, and it works for the homeowner as a round number to shop other companies against. Nothing about the number says which containment, which demo, or which extras it was built for.

The number was set for one job — commonly a small, contained area like a closet or bath, roughly 80 sq ft, one containment zone, no demolition, one HEPA and dehumidifier day, no clearance test, no HVAC cleaning, and no dumpster — and then quoted to every caller afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the special was priced on.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter affected square footage and containment zones, demolition square footage, HEPA and dehumidifier days, clearance testing, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, and an occupied home as their own line items, plus your crew's loaded wage, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into the price, the crew hours, and a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this job, not the closet the special was built on.

What a flat $999 special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the job is an 80 sq ft closet with one containment zone or an 800 sq ft finished basement with two zones and 240 sq ft of demo. Prices extra square footage, containment zones, and demo as their own hour and material lines, so a bigger, harder job returns a bigger number instead of the same one.
Has no line for a clearance test, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, or an occupied home — a fully-loaded basement job prices the same as a bare closet. Adds clearance hours and fee, HVAC hours and cost, dumpster hours and fee, and occupied-home hours only when that scope is turned on, so a loaded job shows up in the price instead of being absorbed into it.
Was priced once, on one closet, and never re-derived from affected area, zones, or extras — it is a marketing number, not a cost-basis number. Recomputes crew hours and materials from the exact area, zones, demo, and extras entered every time, so the price tracks the job rather than a memory of the postcard rate.
On this calculator's own 80 sq ft closet preset — the exact job the $999 number is named for — the flat special already sits $207.55 below that job's own walk-away cost, before a dollar of profit. Returns a walk-away cost of $1,206.55 and a bid price of $1,723.64 for that same closet, at this tool's own shop-rate defaults and a 30% target margin.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away cost, the bid price, and the crew hours, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

Two jobs, the same containment-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($45/hr crew wage, 36% burden, $145 travel and equipment, 18% overhead, a 30% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceA flat $999 specialGap
80 sq ft closet, 1 zone, 1 equipment day — the job the flat number is named for$1,723.64 bid price; $1,206.55 break-even cost$999.00The flat special runs $207.55 under this job's own break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $724.64 under the calculator's own bid price — even on the exact job it claims to price.
800 sq ft finished basement, 2 zones, 4 dry-out days, 240 sq ft demo, clearance, HVAC, dumpster, occupied$11,543.43 bid price; $8,080.40 break-even cost$999.00The same $999 special quotes $7,081.40 below this job's own break-even cost, and $10,544.43 below the calculator's bid price.

Both flat-rate rows use the literal $999 figure named in the calculator's own worked preset, applied to each job as a flat price regardless of containment, demo, or extras. Even the smallest, cheapest job the number is named for already loses money before profit is counted; a bigger remediation turns the same number into a five-figure loss. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one closet it was built on, and nothing about a postcard rate tells a company or a homeowner when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $999 mold special get a remediation job wrong?

Because the cost driver is containment zones, demo, dry-out days, and extras, not "a mold job" alone. An 80 sq ft closet with one containment zone and one equipment day needs a fraction of the labor and material that an 800 sq ft finished basement needs, with two containment zones, four dry-out days, 240 sq ft of demo, a clearance test, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, and an occupied home -- none of which scale with a flat marketed price. A $999 special charges both the same.

What job is the $999 number actually built around?

One specific job: a small, contained area like a closet or bath, roughly 80 sq ft, one containment zone, no demolition, one HEPA and dehumidifier day, no clearance test, no HVAC cleaning, and no dumpster. It is a marketing price meant to get the phone to ring, not a number derived from any particular home's containment, demo, or extras.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($45/hr crew wage, 36% burden, $145 travel and equipment, 18% overhead, a 30% target margin): even the 80 sq ft closet the $999 number is named for has a walk-away cost of $1,206.55 and a bid price of $1,723.64 -- the flat special already sits $207.55 below that job's own break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $724.64 below the calculator's own bid price. Applied to an 800 sq ft finished basement with two containment zones, four dry-out days, 240 sq ft of demo, a clearance test, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, and an occupied home, the same $999 special is $7,081.40 below that job's own $8,080.40 walk-away cost, and $10,544.43 below the calculator's own bid price.

Is a flat mold special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of jobs close to the one the special was built around -- a small, contained area, one zone, no demo, no clearance test, no HVAC cleaning, no dumpster -- a flat number can land close, though on this calculator's own worked example even that job already runs under cost. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard price does not know which band a given job is in and neither does the crew until affected area, zones, demo, and extras are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor or equipment rates. It takes the affected square footage, containment zones, demo, HEPA and dehumidifier days, clearance testing, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, occupancy, and your own crew wage, burden, and overhead, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

vs-xactimate.html.text:
← Mold Remediation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Xactimate

Two different shapes: Xactimate prices an insurance claim against a standardized, shared regional line-item list. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this remediation job cost, given its zones, demo, dry-out days, and access, before you quote it directly.

What each tool is for

Xactimate is line-item estimating software from Xactware, a company founded in 1986 and headquartered in Orem, Utah, acquired by ISO / Verisk in 2006. Insurance adjusters and restoration contractors use it to scope and price a covered loss — water, fire, mold, and similar claims — against a shared, regionally-priced list of standardized line items, so both sides of a claim can negotiate from the same reference prices. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account, and Xactware does not publish a fixed public price for it, so no dollar figure for Xactimate is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — insurance-claim estimating software built around a shared regional price list — are stated, and no dollar amount for Xactimate appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Xactimate does. It has no regional price list, produces no carrier-facing claim estimate, and stores no customer or claim record on a server. It takes job type (closet, bedroom, basement, or sewage-affected), affected square footage, extra containment zones over the included setup, demolition square feet, HEPA and dehumidifier days, third-party clearance testing, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, occupied-home access, loaded wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, the price per square foot of affected area, and where the crew hours are actually going — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines, a deposit split, a price-held date, and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Many remediators get different value from each: Xactimate (or a comparable claims-estimating platform) for scoping and negotiating an insurance-covered loss against a carrier's shared price list, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one job should cost from its own zones, demo, and dry-out days — whether that job is retail, cash, or a supplement check before submitting a claim line. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a claim estimate, an inspection, or a signed proposal, and neither this calculator nor Xactimate performs a mold protocol, a health assessment, or a clearance determination.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or Xactimate?

They price different kinds of jobs. Xactimate is line-item estimating software from Xactware, a company founded in 1986 and based in Orem, Utah, acquired by ISO / Verisk in 2006. Insurance adjusters and restoration contractors use it to scope and price a covered loss against a standardized, regionally-priced list of line items that both sides can point to during a claim negotiation. It is sold as a subscription account, and Xactware does not publish a fixed public price for it, so no dollar figure for Xactimate is stated here — only its well-documented identity and category: insurance-claim estimating software built around a shared regional price list. This calculator does a narrower, different job: starting from job type, affected area, containment zones, demolition square feet, HEPA and dehumidifier days, clearance testing, HVAC cleaning, a dumpster, and occupied-home access, it turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, the price per square foot of affected area, and where the crew hours actually go, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A remediator scoping and negotiating an insurance-covered loss against a carrier's price list needs Xactimate or a comparable claims-estimating platform; a remediator pricing a retail, cash, or negotiated job directly with a homeowner — or checking a bid against their own labor and equipment costs before submitting a claim supplement — is in the right place here.
